content: Sickle cell disease is a genetic blood disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. It is one of the most common genetic blood conditions globally. Acute chest syndrome is a frequent and serious complication of sickle cell disease, representing a significant cause of illness and the leading cause of death in children with this condition. Standard treatments for acute chest syndrome often include intravenous hydration, oxygen therapy to address hypoxia, antibiotics to treat potential infections, and, in some cases, blood transfusions. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of blood transfusions, both simple and exchange transfusions, in treating acute chest syndrome. The goal was to compare the improvement in symptoms and clinical outcomes of blood transfusion therapy against standard care without transfusions. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of relevant databases and journals, with the most recent search completed on May 30, 2019. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared simple or exchange transfusions to standard care in individuals with sickle cell disease experiencing acute chest syndrome. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria for this review. This multicenter trial enrolled 237 participants with various forms of sickle cell disease (169 with SS genotype, 42 with SC genotype, 15 with Sβ⁰-thalassemia, and 11 with Sβ⁺-thalassemia). However, most participants were assigned to an observational arm, and only ten individuals were randomized for the study. Of these, four participants were assigned to the transfusion group and received a single transfusion of 7 to 13 mL/kg of packed red blood cells, while six participants were assigned to the standard care group. In the transfusion group, none of the four participants developed acute chest syndrome. In contrast, two out of six participants (33%) in the standard care group developed acute chest syndrome. However, no data were available for any of the predefined outcomes, limiting the ability to draw robust conclusions. The authors concluded that the evidence from this single, small randomized controlled trial is insufficient to make reliable recommendations regarding the use of blood transfusions for treating acute chest syndrome in individuals with sickle cell disease. While there is some suggestion that chronic blood transfusions may reduce the incidence of acute chest syndrome, there is currently no strong evidence to confirm or refute the benefits of blood transfusions as a treatment option. Additionally, there is very limited information on the potential risks associated with these interventions or guidance to inform clinical decision-making. Clinicians are advised to base treatment decisions on their clinical expertise, the specific circumstances of the patient, and the informed preferences of individuals with sickle cell disease who are experiencing acute chest syndrome. This review underscores the urgent need for high-quality research to provide reliable evidence on the effectiveness and safety of blood transfusions for managing acute chest syndrome in this population.
